question: A digital image a[m,n] in a 2D discrete space is derived from a continuous analog image through which process?
options: An optical averaging process called integration
A quantization process that assigns gray levels
A sampling process commonly called digitization
A Fourier transformation of the continuous image
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2, page 2
source_excerpt: A digital image a[m,n] described in a 2D discrete space is derived from an analog image a(x,y) in a 2D continuous space through a sampling process that is frequently referred to as digitization.

question: In a digitized image divided into rows and columns, what is the intersection of a row and a column called?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2, page 2
source_excerpt: The 2D continuous image a(x,y) is divided into N rows and M columns. The intersection of a row and a column is termed a pixel.

question: Representing the amplitude at a coordinate as an integer value with L different gray levels is called what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2, page 3
source_excerpt: The process of representing the amplitude of the 2D signal at a given coordinate as an integer value with L different gray levels is usually referred to as amplitude quantization or simply quantization.

question: According to the text, what is an image with B = 1 called?
options: A color image with three channels
A binary image with two gray levels
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2, page 4
source_excerpt: When B>1 we speak of a gray-level image; when B=1 we speak of a binary image. In a binary image there are just two gray levels which can be referred to, for example, as black and white or 0 and 1.

question: Which type of operation produces an output value that depends only on the input value at the same coordinate?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.2.1, page 4
source_excerpt: Point - the output value at a specific coordinate is dependent only on the input value at that same coordinate.

question: Which statement characterizes a global image operation?
options: Output depends on all values in the input image
Output depends only on the same pixel
Output depends on a small neighborhood
Output is independent of the input image
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.2.1, page 4
source_excerpt: Global - the output value at a specific coordinate is dependent on all the values in the input image.

question: Which neighborhood is associated with hexagonal sampling?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.2.2, page 5
source_excerpt: Some of the most common neighborhoods are the 4-connected neighborhood and the 8-connected neighborhood in the case of rectangular sampling and the 6-connected neighborhood in the case of hexagonal sampling illustrated in Figure 3.

question: Why are the scan lines of a video image interlaced?
options: To increase the number of color channels
To reduce the perception of flicker
To double the number of image rows
To remove motion blur from the image
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.3, page 6
source_excerpt: The reason for interlacing the scan lines of a video image is to reduce the perception of flicker in a displayed image.

question: The relation c = a convolved with b = b convolved with a demonstrates which property of convolution?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.2, page 7
source_excerpt: Convolution is commutative.

question: Convolution in the spatial domain is equivalent to what operation in the Fourier domain?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 10
source_excerpt: In words, convolution in the spatial domain is equivalent to multiplication in the Fourier (frequency) domain and vice-versa.

question: The Fourier transform represents a signal as a weighted sum of what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.3, page 7
source_excerpt: The Fourier transform produces another representation of a signal, specifically a representation as a weighted sum of complex exponentials.

question: The forward Fourier transform maps the spatial domain to which domain?
options: A discrete spatial domain with integer pixels
A color domain with three channels
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.3, page 8
source_excerpt: the forward transform goes from the spatial domain (either continuous or discrete) to the frequency domain which is always continuous.

question: The statement that the Fourier transform and its inverse are linear operations describes which property?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 9
source_excerpt: The Fourier and the inverse Fourier transforms are linear operations.

question: If a 2D signal is real and even, what is true of its Fourier transform?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 9
source_excerpt: If a 2D signal is real and even, then the Fourier transform is real and even.

question: The discrete-space Fourier transform A(Ω,Ψ) is periodic in both variables with what period?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 9
source_excerpt: The Fourier transform in discrete space, A(Ω,Ψ), is periodic in both Ω and Ψ. Both periods are 2π.

question: According to Parseval's theorem, where can the energy of a signal be measured?
options: In either the spatial or frequency domain
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 10
source_excerpt: The energy, E, in a signal can be measured either in the spatial domain or the frequency domain.

question: If a[m,n] represents a photon count, the physical energy is proportional to what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4, page 10
source_excerpt: If, for example, the value a[m,n] represents a photon count, then the physical energy is proportional to the amplitude, a, and not the square of the amplitude.

question: What is required for complete reconstruction of an image from its Fourier transform?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4.1, page 11
source_excerpt: Both the magnitude and the phase functions are necessary for the complete reconstruction of an image from its Fourier transform.

question: The Fourier transform of a circularly symmetric 2D signal depends only on what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4.2, page 13
source_excerpt: The Fourier transform of a circularly symmetric 2D signal is a function of only the radial frequency, q. The dependence on the angular frequency, ξ, has vanished.

question: Which function appears in the Hankel transform used for circularly symmetric signals?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4.2, page 12
source_excerpt: Jo(•) is a Bessel function of the first kind of order zero.

question: In the text's terminology, what is the relationship between the PSF and the OTF?
options: PSF is in frequency; OTF is in space
Both terms refer to the spatial domain
PSF is spatial; OTF is its Fourier transform
OTF is the inverse of the PSF in space
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.4.3, page 13
source_excerpt: we will refer to a spatial domain term as the point spread function (PSF) or the 2D impulse response and its Fourier transforms as the optical transfer function (OTF) or simply transfer function.

question: As the brightness value a increases from –∞ to +∞, what range does P(a) cover?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.1, page 13
source_excerpt: As a increases from – ∞ to + ∞, P(a) increases from 0 to 1. P(a) is monotonic, non-decreasing in a and thus dP/da ≥ 0.

question: In the text, what is p(a) called in the expression p(a)Δa?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.2, page 13
source_excerpt: The probability that a brightness in a region falls between a and a+Δa, given the probability distribution function P(a), can be expressed as p(a)Δa where p(a) is the probability density function:

question: Which statement describes a local image operation?
options: Output depends only on the same pixel
Output depends on all image pixels
Output is independent of the input
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.2.2, page 5
source_excerpt: Local operations produce an output pixel value b[m=mo,n=no] based upon the pixel values in the neighborhood of a[m=mo,n=no].

question: For the same video camera, why can different frame grabbers produce different numbers of columns per line?
options: Because the number of rows changes
Because the display refresh rate changes
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 2.3, page 6
source_excerpt: Different frame grabbers for the same video camera might produce M = 384, 512, or 768 columns (pixels) per line.

question: How is the average brightness of a region defined in the text?
options: The sample mean of pixel brightnesses
The largest brightness value observed anywhere in the region
The brightness value that occurs most frequently in the region
The middle value after sorting all pixel brightnesses
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.3, page 17
source_excerpt: The average brightness of a region is defined as the sample mean of the pixel brightnesses within that region.

question: The sample standard deviation sa is an estimate of what?
options: The standard deviation of the underlying brightness distribution
The number of pixels in the region
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.4, page 17
source_excerpt: The standard deviation, sa, is an estimate of σa of the underlying brightness probability distribution.

question: In the text's percentile definitions, what does the 0% percentile represent?
options: The minimum value in the region
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.6, page 18
source_excerpt: 0% the minimum value in the region

question: Which percentile corresponds to the median value in a region?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.6, page 18
source_excerpt: 50% the median value in the region

question: What is the mode of a brightness distribution?
options: The average of the brightest pixels
The difference between maximum and minimum
The median of the lowest half
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.7, page 18
source_excerpt: The mode of the distribution is the most frequent brightness value. There is no guarantee that a mode exists or that it is unique.

question: In the signal-to-noise ratio definitions, what characterizes the noise?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.8, page 18
source_excerpt: The noise is characterized by its standard deviation, sn.

question: How is the brightness probability density function frequently estimated?
options: By counting occurrences of each brightness and forming a histogram
By applying a two-dimensional Fourier transform to the entire image region
By locating only the maximum brightness value in the image
By sorting the image rows according to their average brightness
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.5.2, page 16
source_excerpt: The brightness probability density function is frequently estimated by counting the number of times that each brightness occurs in the region to generate a histogram, h[a].

question: For the standard chain code, what is a contour pixel?
options: Any pixel that has the maximum brightness value within the entire image
A pixel located only on the outer border of the image frame
A pixel that has no connected neighbors in any direction at all
An object pixel with a background pixel among its 4-connected neighbors
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.6.1, page 20
source_excerpt: For the standard implementation of the chain code we consider a contour pixel to be an object pixel that has a background (non-object) pixel as one or more of its 4-connected neighbors.

question: What directions do the even chain codes 0, 2, 4, and 6 represent?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.6.2, page 20
source_excerpt: Even codes {0,2,4,6} correspond to horizontal and vertical directions; odd codes {1,3,5,7} correspond to the diagonal directions.

question: Each chain code represents an angular direction in multiples of how many degrees?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.6.2, page 20
source_excerpt: Each code can be considered as the angular direction, in multiples of 45 °, that we must move to go from one contour pixel to the next.

question: How many possible directions does the crack code use?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.6.3, page 21
source_excerpt: The crack code can be viewed as a chain code with four possible directions instead of eight.

question: What does a run code give for a consecutive group of object pixels along a row?
options: Its distance from the image center
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 3.6.4, page 21
source_excerpt: A third representation is based on coding the consecutive pixels along a row, a run, that belong to an object by giving the starting position of the run and the ending position of the run.

question: The Weber-Fechner law says the visual response is approximately proportional to what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.1.2, page 22
source_excerpt: to a good approximation, the visual response, R, is proportional to the logarithm of the intensity. This is known as the Weber-Fechner law.

question: What does the Mach band effect produce at a step edge in brightness?
options: A complete loss of edge detail
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.1.2, page 23
source_excerpt: The total effect is one of increased, local, perceived contrast at a step edge in brightness.

question: At a viewing distance of 50 cm, what spatial frequency gives the maximum response?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.2, page 24
source_excerpt: The spatial frequency that will give maximum response is at 10 cycles per degree.

question: According to the text, human physical color perception is based on what?
options: Four color channels in the lens
Two opponent channels in the cortex
Three color pigments in the retina
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.3, page 24
source_excerpt: The physical perception of color is based upon three color pigments in the retina.

question: What information is lost when converting tristimulus values to CIE chromaticity coordinates?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.3.2, page 25
source_excerpt: The tristimulus values are linear in I(λ) and thus the absolute intensity information has been lost in the calculation of the chromaticity coordinates { x,y}.

question: What property is approximated by the (u',v') chromaticity space?
options: A linear relation between brightness and voltage
Small coordinate changes produce equally small perceived color changes
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 4.3.2, page 27
source_excerpt: Small changes almost anywhere in the (u',v') chromaticity space produce equally small changes in the perceived colors.

question: If a lens does not meet the circularly symmetric, aberration-free, diffraction-limited assumptions, what happens to its cutoff frequencies?
options: They become higher than the diffraction-limited values
They are lower than the diffraction-limited values
They become independent of the lens
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 5.1, page 29
source_excerpt: If the lens does not meet one or more of these assumptions then it will still be bandlimited but at lower cutoff frequencies than those given in eq. (57).

question: When does the sampling aperture have only a marginal effect on the final signal?
options: When the bandlimited and Nyquist conditions are satisfied
When the aperture is much wider than the sampling interval
When the image contains no noise
When the sensor has a binary output
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 5.1.1, page 30
source_excerpt: The aperture p(x,y) described above will have only a marginal effect on the final signal if the two conditions eqs. (56) and (57) are satisfied.

question: For image analysis, the sampling density should be based on what?
options: The desired measurement accuracy and precision
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 5.2.3, page 32
source_excerpt: If one is interested in image analysis, one should choose a sampling density based upon the desired measurement accuracy (bias) and precision (CV).

question: What probability distribution describes the number of photons counted in an observation window?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 6.1, page 33
source_excerpt: The probability distribution for p photons in an observation window of length T seconds is known to be Poisson.

question: What is an effective way to reduce thermal electrons that cause dark current?
options: Reducing the number of gray levels
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 6.2, page 33
source_excerpt: By cooling the CCD chip it is possible to reduce significantly the number of thermal electrons that give rise to thermal noise or dark current.

question: KTC noise is associated with what component?
options: The gate capacitor of an FET
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 6.4, page 34
source_excerpt: Noise associated with the gate capacitor of an FET is termed KTC noise and can be non-negligible.

question: Where does quantization noise occur?
options: In the optical lens system before the sensor
In the ADC during amplitude quantization
In the display refresh circuit after conversion
In the camera shutter mechanism during exposure
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 6.6, page 35
source_excerpt: Quantization noise is inherent in the amplitude quantization process and occurs in the analog-to-digital converter, ADC.

question: In the camera model c = gain multiplied by a to the power gamma plus offset, what is required for a truly linear recording system?
options: Gamma equal to zero and offset equal to one
Gamma equal to one and offset equal to one
Gamma equal to one and offset equal to zero
Gamma equal to any value with zero offset
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.1, page 36
source_excerpt: For a truly linear recording system we must have γ = 1 and offset = 0.

question: What does absolute sensitivity measure?
options: The minimum number of detectable photoelectrons
The maximum number of electrons that a CCD well can hold
The total number of gray levels produced by the ADC
The number of pixels read from the sensor each second
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.2, page 36
source_excerpt: First, we can determine the minimum number of detectable photoelectrons. This can be termed the absolute sensitivity.

question: Relative sensitivity describes the number of photoelectrons needed to do what?
options: Change the exposure time by one second
Change from one digital brightness level to the next
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.2, page 36
source_excerpt: Second, we can describe the number of photoelectrons necessary to change from one digital brightness level to the next, that is, to change one analog-to-digital unit (ADU). This can be termed the relative sensitivity.

question: What does quantum efficiency describe?
options: The number of pixels in a CCD row
The average number of photoelectrons produced per photon at a wavelength
The ratio of readout rate to frame rate
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.2.2, page 37
source_excerpt: The quantum efficiency refers to how many photoelectrons are produced—on the average—per photon at a given wavelength.

question: What limits the maximum SNR per pixel in a CCD camera?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.3.2, page 39
source_excerpt: The pixels in CCD cameras have, however, a finite well capacity. This finite capacity, C, means that the maximum SNR for a CCD camera per pixel is given by:

question: What does shading mean in the text?
options: A constant input produces a constant digital image
The camera always saturates at the maximum level
The image histogram is perfectly equalized
A constant physical input produces a nonconstant digital image
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.4, page 39
source_excerpt: By this we mean that if the physical input image a(x,y) = constant, then the digital version of the image will not be constant.

question: What is the fill factor of a CCD sensor?
options: The fraction of the surface that is sensitive to light
The average number of photoelectrons produced for each analog-to-digital unit
The ratio of the camera readout rate to the display refresh rate
The maximum number of bits that can be stored for each image pixel
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.5.2, page 41
source_excerpt: The fraction of the surface that is sensitive to light is termed the fill factor

question: An IR blocking filter used with a silicon CCD blocks wavelengths above what value?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 7.6, page 42
source_excerpt: This filter blocks wavelengths above 750 nm. and thus prevents fogging of the image from the longer wavelengths found in sunlight.

question: What is the standard interlace for video systems?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 8.2, page 44
source_excerpt: Standard interlace for video systems is 2:1.

question: What interlace is used when the refresh rate is above 60 images per second?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 8.2, page 44
source_excerpt: Since interlacing is not necessary at refresh rates above 60 images/s, an interlace of 1:1 is used with such systems.

question: What display resolution corresponds to standard printing conventions in the text?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 8.3, page 44
source_excerpt: It is relatively straightforward to obtain display systems with a resolution of 72 spots per inch (28.3 spots per cm.)

question: In basic contrast stretching, the 100% brightness value is mapped to what value?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.1.1, page 45
source_excerpt: then one generally maps the 0% value (or minimum as defined in Section 3.5.2) to the value 0 and the 100% value (or maximum) to the value 2 B–1.

question: What histogram does histogram equalization try to produce?
options: A histogram with only two levels
A histogram that matches the input exactly
A histogram with a single peak at zero
A constant histogram in which all brightness values are equally probable
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.1.2, page 46
source_excerpt: The most common histogram normalization technique is histogram equalization where one attempts to change the histogram through the use of a function b = ƒ( a) into a histogram that is constant for all brightness values. This would correspond to a brightness distribution where all values are equally probable.

question: For histogram equalization, what must be true of a suitable function f?
options: It must be linear and decreasing
It must be periodic with period B
It must be differentiable with df/da greater than or equal to zero
It must map every input to the same output
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.1.2, page 46
source_excerpt: From eq. (79) we see that suitable means that ƒ(•) is differentiable and that dƒ/da ≥ 0.

question: Which local filters can be driven by a histogram from a local region?
options: Only Fourier-domain lowpass filters applied to the whole image
Only binary XOR filters applied to pairs of image pixels
Only recursive Gaussian filters applied along image rows
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.1.3, page 47
source_excerpt: Examples include minimum filtering, median filtering, and maximum filtering [23].

question: Which binary operation can remove objects that have already been analyzed from a region of interest?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.2.1, page 47
source_excerpt: The SUB operation can be particularly useful when the image a represents a region-of-interest that we want to analyze systematically and the image b represents objects that, having been analyzed, can now be discarded, that is, subtracted, from the region.

question: Which arithmetic operation is defined as c = a / b?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.2.2, page 49
source_excerpt: DIV c = a / b floating point

question: In convolution, what is the output pixel value?
options: The weighted sum of input pixels within the window
The maximum input pixel within the window
The median input pixel within the window
The unweighted first pixel in the window
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3, page 49
source_excerpt: The output pixel value is the weighted sum of the input pixels within the window where the weights are the values of the filter assigned to every pixel of the window itself.

question: What is the impulse response of an LSI imaging system called?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3.1, page 50
source_excerpt: If an impulse point of light δ(x,y) is imaged through an LSI system then the impulse response of that system is called the point spread function (PSF).

question: The optical transfer function is the Fourier transform of what?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3.1, page 50
source_excerpt: The Fourier transform of the PSF is called the optical transfer function (OTF).

question: When a convolution window extends outside the image, what does the text say about assigning values outside the boundaries?
options: Only zero padding is mathematically valid
The filter must be shrunk to one pixel
One of several standard extension conventions may be chosen
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3.2, page 52
source_excerpt: The standard alternatives are a) extend the images with a constant (possibly zero) brightness value, b) extend the image periodically, c) extend the image by mirroring it at its boundaries, or d) extend the values at the boundaries indefinitely.

question: What is the spatial-domain computational complexity per pixel for a J by K convolution kernel?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3.2, page 52
source_excerpt: The computational complexity for a J×K convolution kernel implemented in the spatial domain on an image of N × N is O(J⋅K)

question: For a separable kernel, what does the spatial-domain complexity per pixel become?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.3.2, page 53
source_excerpt: For an N × N image this, in general, reduces the computational complexity per pixel from O(J⋅K) to O(J+K).

question: How are weights assigned within the support of a uniform smoothing filter?
options: All values receive the same weight
Weights decrease linearly from the center
Only the center value is nonzero
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.4.1, page 55
source_excerpt: The output image is based on a local averaging of the input filter where all of the values within the filter support have the same weight.

question: What key implementation property does the text state for the Gaussian filter?
options: It requires a circular support only
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.4.1, page 56
source_excerpt: The Gaussian filter is separable:

question: What can derivative algorithms provide for a digitized image?
options: Exact analytical derivatives of the continuous image
Approximations to the true spatial derivatives
Only Fourier transforms with no spatial meaning
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.5, page 61
source_excerpt: As a result the algorithms we will present can only be seen as approximations to the true spatial derivatives of the original spatially-continuous image.

question: Taking a spatial derivative emphasizes what in the resulting image?
source: Fundamentals of Image Processing, Young, Gerbrands and van Vliet, Version 2.3 (2007), Section 9.5, page 61
source_excerpt: This means that high frequency noise will be emphasized in the resulting image.

question: Where does the magnitude gradient take on large values?
options: Where there are strong edges in the image
